Science.title: Imperial woodpecker returns to life as a detailed digital specimen
Science.summary: Researchers have created a detailed, animated 3D model of the imperial woodpecker (Campephilus imperialis), a spectacular bird that has not been confirmed in the wild since 1956. The model, built from a museum specimen and the only known film footage of the living bird, is freely available to scientists, educators and the public.

Science.title: Electron density check offers better starting point for chemistry's most difficult metal molecules
Science.summary: New materials and catalysts have the potential to transform everything from food production and medicine to batteries and stainless steel. Computer simulations help scientists narrow down promising candidates before testing them in a lab, but those simulations can be unreliable, especially for molecules that contain multiple metals.

Science.title: A forgotten fossil reveals a fearsome dinosaur with giant claws
Science.summary: A 120-million-year-old fossil forgotten in a museum for nearly a century has revealed a terrifying new dinosaur that may have been more dangerous to humans than a T. rex. The tiger-sized predator also provides the first evidence of megaraptorans in Europe, helping explain how these mysterious dinosaurs eventually became gigantic hunters.

Science.title: NASA to Conduct Low-Altitude Flights Over Texas Farmland
Science.summary: A NASA Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Transit, Texas, from Thursday, Oct. 22, through Monday, Nov. 9. These flights will measure gaseous and particulate emissions from animal feeding operations. Agricultural emissions represent an important and understudied part of Earth’s land and atmosphere systems. The FarmFlux mission will deploy […]

Science.title: Lion tracks from the ice age: How two ways of seeing brought ancient animals to life
Science.summary: The coastline near the southern tip of Africa looked vastly different between about 400,000 years ago and 70,000 years ago, compared with today. At times it lay as much as 100km (62 miles) south of its present location, exposing the vast Palaeo-Agulhas Plain, which contained an extensive habitat for large mammals. At other times the sea level was briefly as much as 13 meters (43 feet) higher than today's mean level.

Science.title: Margaret Hamilton obituary: computer scientist who pioneered software engineering and helped us get to the Moon
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03233-6 Programmer whose forward-thinking and reliable code helped to save the Apollo 11 mission.

Science.title: First bacterial galactose oxidase expands toolkit for greener drug and food ingredient production
Science.summary: To produce pharmaceuticals, food ingredients, and flavors and fragrances, it is often necessary to oxidize alcohols. In conventional chemistry, this transformation typically relies on harsh oxidants and elevated temperatures and generates toxic waste.

Science.title: Silicon qubits surpass 99.99% gate fidelity while operating three at once
Science.summary: Silicon spin qubits are a promising platform for building scalable quantum computers as they are compatible with the semiconductor manufacturing technologies used to produce today's computer chips. However, they have an important weakness: silicon spin qubits typically lose accuracy when several qubits are under parallel control. To be useful, quantum computers will need to operate many qubits simultaneously without compromising the accuracy of their operations.

Science.title: Give me the good news: four science stories to brighten your day
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03152-6 Drugs that can reverse multiple sclerosis in mice and a new species of penguin are just the beginning.

Science.title: Molecular snapshots reveal how viral enzymes switch between inserting and removing DNA
Science.summary: Bacteriophages, or viruses that infect bacteria, have a fiendishly simple purpose in life: attach to a bacterial cell, inject their DNA and then use the host's genetic machinery to reproduce. In doing so, they may have evolved some of the most efficient gene-editing tools ever seen in nature.

Science.title: Arctic sea ice hits another troubling low in 2026
Science.summary: Arctic sea ice is shrinking in both winter and summer, with satellite records revealing that the region's remaining ice is becoming thinner, younger, and more vulnerable to melting. Despite a recent slowdown in summer losses, scientists warn that the Arctic could experience a nearly ice-free summer before 2050.

Science.title: Researchers find that some weeds get supercharged by an indirect hit of herbicide
Science.summary: A brush with low doses of the herbicide dicamba spurs oxalis, a weed commonly known as wood sorrel, to produce more flowers, University of Michigan researchers have discovered. The finding suggests that farmers and homeowners are inadvertently making weeds growing around the perimeter of their fields or lawns stronger, the researchers say. The study results are published in the journal New Phytologist.

Science.title: In animated films, nonhuman characters are still overwhelmingly male
Science.summary: Female protagonists in animated films have come a long way over the past several decades. Take the 1959 movie "Sleeping Beauty": Soft-spoken and vulnerable, Princess Aurora is cursed as an infant by the evil fairy Maleficent and ultimately saved not by her own wits, but by a prince's kiss.

Science.title: Vaonis unveils Atlas, the world's 1st modular smart telescope system
Science.summary: Pre-orders are now open for the Atlas, the new modular smart telescope from Vaonis which allows observation with two optical tubes.

Science.title: Mysterious hole in Neanderthal shoulder blade may have been a 'kill shot' from a wooden spear, according to archaeologists
Science.summary: A rare discovery reveals that 75,000 years ago, a Neanderthal from Shanidar Cave in Iraq died a grisly death, likely from a wooden spear.

Science.title: Baby lobster decline foreshadows major midcoast population losses, study shows
Science.summary: A steep drop in baby lobsters provided an early warning of the sharp decline in adult lobsters along Maine's midcoast, a new University of Maine study shows.

Science.title: Six lessons to improve leadership opportunities for women with disability
Science.summary: Employers must do more to remove the barriers preventing women with disability from progressing into leadership, according to a new report from People with Disability Australia (PWDA), the national disability rights and advocacy organization. Researchers identify six lessons to help drive change.

Science.title: Single 2D crystal transforms into transistor with built-in insulation and electrical contacts
Science.summary: A transistor normally requires several fundamentally different materials—a semiconductor to carry current, an insulating dielectric to control it and metallic contacts through which current enters and leaves. Integrating all of these components becomes increasingly difficult as semiconductor devices approach the atomic scale.

Science.title: Beat light pollution with these six portable telescopes
Science.summary: Sick of skyglow spoiling your stargazing? These six telescopes are portable enough that you can easily pack them away and seek out darker skies.

Science.title: Retail research shifted in five ways, study finds
Science.summary: Retail research has changed during the last couple of decades, according to an analysis of almost 5,200 papers covering business practices, consumer behavior and technology. The study, published in the International Journal of Electronic Marketing and Retailing, considered papers from the four leading specialist journals in this area.

Science.title: Better together? Coral fusion could throw bleached reefs a lifeline
Science.summary: When corals are stressed by pollution, high water temperatures or other environmental changes, they can lose the microscopic algae living inside them and on which they depend for food. As a result, they turn white, a phenomenon known as coral bleaching. They will not die straight away, but it will be game over if the stress continues long enough for them to starve.

Science.title: Chronic back pain may activate an unexpected brain network, study finds
Science.summary: Movement-induced flares in chronic back pain activate brain regions involved in self-reflection, suggesting chronic pain may be processed differently than acute pain.

Science.title: DNA from centuries-old skeletons buried in Montreal reveals no genetic mixing between Indigenous people and French colonists
Science.summary: A study of DNA from early colonial-era skeletons in a Montreal cemetery has revealed that none of them had any Indigenous ancestry.

Science.title: NASA's SkyFall helicopters will 'show us parts of Mars we've never seen before', scientists say
Science.summary: "Just like here on Earth, Mars helicopters can cover distance quickly and can go places that might be impossible to reach by ground."

Science.title: The little‑known 14th-century battle that has shaped English, Scottish and French relations
Science.summary: On Oct. 17, 1346, the Battle of Neville's Cross was fought outside Durham in the northeast of England. It was a decisive moment in Anglo-Scottish history that led to the capture of King David II of Scotland. Yet few have heard of it.

Science.title: 'Dungeon Crawler Carl' author Matt Dinniman talks inspirations, success, and the upcoming Peacock TV series (interview)
Science.summary: 'Luckily I’m still in love with this story, and I am in love with writing it.'

Science.title: Tapeworm drug could help treat endometriosis, mouse study hints
Science.summary: A recent study in mice hints that a modified tapeworm medicine might help relieve painful lesions seen in endometriosis.

Science.title: Testosterone for menopause: The treatment is rising in popularity, but does it work?
Science.summary: Women are using testosterone in the hope that it will treat their menopause symptoms, but little evidence supports the approach, experts say.
